To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the future of Australian agriculture is likely to be determined by a combination of: (i) the ability of the sector to increase its productivity and competitiveness; (ii) the ability of Australian agriculture to attract and retain a skilled workforce; and (iii) the capacity of agriculture to respond to climate change.
• The rate of growth in productivity in agriculture has slowed in recent decades.
• The rate of growth in agricultural TFP in Australia over the past 25 years has been around 1.5% per annum, but this has slowed to around 1.0%.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1.

the question of what are the likely drivers of productivity in agriculture over the coming two decades, and what are the implications of these trends for the future competitiveness and viability of Australian agriculture.
the future productivity challenge for Australian agriculture, and the prospects for the sector to meet this challenge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Australia has a productivity problem, but that the problem is not necessarily insurmountable.

Australia has the potential for a strong and competitive agricultural industry, but that this will require significant investment in R&D and other areas to ensure that the productivity growth of the industry continues to outperform the rest of the economy.
Australia has a major productivity and competitiveness challenge in agriculture over the period to at least 2020 and probably to 2030.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the future of Australian agriculture depends critically upon the ability to maintain a rate of productivity growth at least in the 2% range and preferably closer to the 2.5 – 3% range.
there are some very real challenges for agriculture to remain competitive and productive.
there are a number of factors that will impact on the future growth of agricultural productivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the productivity growth challenge for Australian agriculture is a significant one and that there is a need for a concerted effort by all stakeholders to address the challenge.
there is a need to return to the level of investment in agricultural R & D seen in the 1960s if we are to maintain our current competitiveness and productivity growth.
the future competitiveness of Australian agriculture is very much at risk if productivity growth rates do not recover to the long term trend rate.
